common_name: Renata Schefflera (Glossy Compact Dwarf Umbrella Tree)

planting.note: Plant outdoors after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 grow in containers moved outside for the warm season and brought in before temperatures drop below 35F in fall. In zone 10-11 it can stay outdoors year-round as a dense landscape shrub.

directions: Renata is a solid deep-green, non-variegated dwarf umbrella tree selection, lacking the cream or gold splashing found on Trinette, Gold Capella, and Janine, and it tends to hold a denser, more compact branching habit with tighter clusters of glossy leaflets than the plain species. Because it carries no variegation to lose, it grows a shade faster and more evenly in lower light than its variegated siblings, making it a dependable choice for a uniformly dark green shade hedge or floor specimen. Its palmate leaves are made up of 7-9 leathery, oval leaflets radiating umbrella-style from the leaf stalk. Prune stem tips in spring to keep growth bushy, and grow in bright indirect light to partial shade in well-drained, humus-rich soil.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Bicolor is more vigorous than the Colorama and Tricolor selections and tolerates slightly lower light while still showing its margin color.

directions: Bicolor carries a simpler two-tone pattern than the multi-striped Tricolor or the pink-heavy Colorama: each narrow, arching leaf shows a solid green-and-cream center split lengthwise, edged on both sides by a thin reddish-burgundy margin that gives the cultivar its name. The color contrast is bolder and more graphic than the softer, more evenly blended striping of Tricolor, though less flamboyant than Colorama's wide pink bands. It keeps the same slow-growing, multi-caned, sculptural silhouette typical of Dracaena marginata as it ages. Water only after the top inch or two of soil dries, use filtered water to avoid fluoride-related leaf-tip burn, and keep it above 55F.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or bright shaded patio container in filtered light in well-drained potting mix; Limelight needs noticeably brighter indirect light than Warneckii or Janet Craig to keep its neon color from fading toward plain green.

directions: Limelight arose as a branch mutation of the striped Warneckii cultivar but lost the white margins entirely, replacing them with an unbroken rosette of vivid, glowing chartreuse-yellow foliage unlike the deep green of Janet Craig or the crisp white stripes of Warneckii. The color is brightest and most saturated in strong filtered light, fading toward a duller yellow-green if grown too dark, so it needs somewhat more light than its darker-leaved fragrans relatives. It forms the same dense, multi-caned clump habit typical of corn plant cultivars. Let the top half of the potting mix dry between waterings and avoid cold drafts below 55F.

common_name: Silver Hahnii Snake Plant (Dwarf Silver-Frosted Rosette Sansevieria)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix; Silver Hahnii's overall pale coloring shows best out of hot direct sun.

directions: Unlike the dark green base color of plain Hahnii or the gold-edged Golden Hahnii, Silver Hahnii's leaves are washed an overall pale silvery gray-green, with only faint, barely visible darker cross-banding showing through, giving the low bird's-nest rosette a frosted, metallic cast that sets it apart from every other Hahnii-type cultivar. It stays as compact as its Hahnii relatives, rarely exceeding a foot across, and suits a small pot, dish garden, or tabletop planting equally well. Its pale color is most pronounced in bright, filtered light. Water only when the soil is fully dry and avoid overpotting, which invites root rot in this slow grower.

planting.note: Grow in a shallow pot of fast-draining succulent mix in bright indirect light; allow the plant's spreading stolons room to send up new rosettes at a distance from the mother plant rather than confining it to a tight pot.

directions: Collected in Kenya and described in 1995, this species grows nothing like the flat fan-shaped rosettes of trifasciata cultivars or the rounded blades of cylindrica: its short, conical, cross-banded leaves stack tightly in rows of five up a compact stem, each tipped with a sharp spine, while pandanus-like stolons creep outward from the base and send up fresh stacked rosettes some distance from the parent, a slow 'walking' habit unique among the species covered here. The leaf margins show a fine reddish-brown edge with a pale membrane near the base. Give it the same bright indirect light and thoroughly-dry-between-waterings regimen as other sansevierias, and let stolon offsets establish undisturbed for several years before dividing.

common_name: Black Gold Snake Plant (Dark Gold-Edged Sansevieria)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix; Black Gold's tall, upright leaves make it better suited to a floor planter than the low dish-garden Hahnii types.

directions: Black Gold's stiffly upright blades are a deep, almost blackish green running the full length of each leaf, bordered by a bright golden-yellow margin, a bolder and more saturated combination than the plain mottled green of the common species or the broader creamy center-stripe of Laurentii. It grows substantially taller than the dwarf Hahnii-type cultivars, reaching several feet in a large container over time, giving it a more architectural, upright presence. Like other snake plants it thrives on neglect. Water only when the soil is fully dry, and avoid overpotting, which encourages root rot in this slow-growing succulent.
